extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, journalism students, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used by television producers and newsmagazine editors to decide which stories to run and how to package them. Covers novelty/timeliness, story quality, balance, technical standards, and competitive considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (timeliness/newness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is part of the definition of news and is circumscribed by the period between the previous and current deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: hard-news film shot a day or two earlier may be used if good; features can 'stay on the shelf' longer because they are timeless. Newsmagazine stories held for space are rewritten before reconsideration; thrice-postponed stories are usually killed. Journalists must also apply other novelty considerations beyond simple recency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging novelty by whether a story is new to the journalists themselves, assuming it will then be new to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists often 'create' novelty by treating events as disparate and ahistorical; some sources may consider items old-hat even if journalists find them novel. Awareness that audiences may have heard headlines via radio or local news affects choices (e.g., using film rather than 'tell' stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: The peg
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a recent event or public official's statement as a 'handle' or peg to make a feature topical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pegs are the primary exclusionary consideration when oversupply of potential stories exists; pegged features are preferred, pegless ones are first eliminated. Pegs can be any recent actor/activity (e.g., start of school year for education features) and are often provided by publicity-seeking sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition taboo
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are judged repetitive if similar ones making the same point have been used within the past twelve to twenty-four months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied differentially: important public figures, dramatic news (natural disasters, battles), and violations of enduring values are often exempt. Repetition taboo protects scarce airtime/print space and is enforced both to avoid audience boredom and peer criticism ('we've-done-it-before' kills stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshness versus staleness
rubrics_metrics.description: A story can be 'fresh' or 'stale'; freshness can be supplied by a new angle, sources, techniques, or metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists search for reporters/filmmakers/writers with fresh approaches; portfolios are reviewed for imaginative work. Freshness is cyclical—actors become familiar, boredom sets in, and coverage declines even if substantive significance remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive freshness (trend spotting risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of novelty and trend stories carries risk if chosen too early or too late relative to the trend's 'ripening, cresting, and declining' curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudent selectors may wait for another medium to take the lead or check with multiple bureaus; choosing too early risks appearing 'too far out' or 'kooky,' too late risks being imitative and harming credibility. Minimal legitimating evidence is often required to justify a trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action (dramatic activity/emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that report dramatic activities or emotions are judged best because action attracts and holds audiences and boosts journalists' morale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action is the most easily recognized 'highlight'; in its absence editors seek substitutes. Action makes coverage straightforward—'you only have to cover it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper narrative or filmic pace keeps the viewer or reader involved when action is scarce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television uses camera angles and cutting to speed slow-paced material; magazines use vivid language and dramatic quotes to interrupt dull narrative ('tick tock'). Interviewers may ask leading questions to elicit dramatic responses to improve pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which all possible angles have been considered, all available sources consulted, all important issues dealt with, and feasible highlights exploited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television also measures completeness by speed of arrival and number of eyewitnesses/victims interviewed on scene; magazines judge by amount of important or interesting detail unearthed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity with parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must make its point quickly ('billboard'), set the scene (establishing shots), and use a logical structure leading to a strong ending ('kicker').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television language must be simple; magazine writers should strategically locate dramatic components between less dramatic ones. The ideal ending should make the audience sit up and take notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esthetic and technical standards (film and print quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical and esthetic standards for film (exposure, synchronization) and for coordinated film-and-text presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underexposed/overexposed or out-of-sync film is killed unless it is an irreplaceable exclusive. Technical standards are peer-set; imperfections undetectable by viewers can still provoke strong peer reactions. Magazine stories are less constrained because text can be rewritten, but printing errors after galleys are problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restaging permissible conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Restaging or reproducing events or rehearsing interviewees is considered permissible only if it does not alter observed events, interviews, or their meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television interviewers may rehearse respondents to obtain shorter, more dramatic on-camera answers; magazine editors shorten/edit quotes ex post facto. Re-enactments for camera (repeating ceremonies) are sometimes used if crews missed the moment but are disliked since participants may be self-conscious; deliberately creating incidents for cameras is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story mixture (program/issue pacing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A news program or magazine issue should present a diverse collection of stories—serious, bad, and lengthy items must be balanced with light, good, and short stories to avoid depressing or boring audience and staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers like to end programs with humorous closers; pacing requirements govern both story selection and grouping into an issue/program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of subject matter within an issue or program is sought; editors avoid running multiple similar-topic items in the same week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may combine similar topics into one story but avoid running, for example, two biographies or two biology stories in the same week; section writers take constituency balance into account (e.g., religion writers balance coverage across faiths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure domestic news originates from all parts of the country to avoid geographic bias, especially New York bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features are sometimes selected because they come from underrepresented communities or states; New York suggestions are downplayed because journalists are overexposed to local happenings, though nationalization (bureau roundups) can mitigate localness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking coverage across demographic groups (age, race, sex) and quoting ordinary people as well as public officials to achieve racial and sexual balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsmagazines look energetically for news about/for young people; section writers consider constituency balance. Racial and sexual balance became a criterion in response to protests; demographic balance often follows outside criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting dominant or most vocal positions and 'both sides' to avoid accusations of bias (reinforced by the FCC Fairness Doctrine in television).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieved by identifying main positions and quoting both sides (Republican/Democratic politicians; environmentalists vs. businessmen). Media sometimes juxtapose stories or kill stories to achieve balance; when overlooked sides protest, the media may adjust coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive exclusivity and scoops
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking exclusives, original feature ideas, and small scoops to differentiate from rivals rather than merely being first with the obvious story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because being first is harder with many reporters present, rivals compete for exclusives and original angles; small details can become the margin of victory. Competition also motivates cover choices and feature prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dyadic competition (rival-focused selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition is largely dyadic (two main rivals), and editors often select or avoid stories based on expectations of what the rival will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rivals (e.g., Time vs. Newsweek, NBC vs. CBS) are watched closely; editors may drop or choose stories to avoid imitation or to match rivals. Mutual expectations can discourage innovation in story selection and contribute to similarity across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover competition and timing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about front-of-book covers are driven by timing, the desire to be first, and concern about imitation; late-breaking stories force editors to weigh extra effort/expense against the risk of being imitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers are exempt from competition if an important story breaks early in the week; last-minute changes may be made if budgets/quality permit. Similar covers can embarrass editors; magazines sometimes run shorter inside stories to admit defeat while blunting the rival's victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition as professional quality control (use of rivals and the Times as standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists use competition and the coverage of rivals—especially The New York Times—as a standard against which to evaluate their own performance and choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uncertain about a selection, editors check how the Times covered the story; competition supplies peer feedback that journalists take seriously, more so than sparse audience feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format/medium fit and technological constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations of medium and format (television vs. magazine, film vs. tape, color photography, live interruptions) are built into story selection and production decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological changes often affect packaging more than content (e.g., shift to color photography to match TV). Television prefers film for big stories to compete with local programs, while videotape live interruptions complicate prescheduling; format constraints can determine whether a story is usable (e.g., unusable poorly exposed film).
